newsitem.title: USA: IBM hits pre-1987 stock market crash highs.
newsitem.headline: IBM hits pre-1987 stock market crash highs.

text.p: Shares of International Business Machines Corp soared to an intra-session high it has not seen since before the October 1987 stock market crash, after Merrill Lynch raised its price target on the stock.
IBM shares climbed 5-1/8 to 142 in heavy volume of over 4.6 million shares. It was the most active issue on the New York Stock Exchange.

An IBM spokesman said the last time IBM shares closed above 140 was sometime in October 1987, before Black Monday when the Dow industrials fell 508 points, a 22.6 percent drop. IBM shares hit a high of 175, post splits, in August, 1987.
The last time IBM's shares closed above 140 was on October 15, 1987. Black Monday occurred on Oct. 19, 1987.

Traders said that the stock's climb was fueled by the bullish comments from influential Merrill Lynch analyst Daniel Mandresh, as well as some recent buying by Fidelity's Magellan Fund. In September, IBM appeared in the top 10 holdings of the Magellan Fund, which is gradually moving to increase its holdings in tech stocks, under its new manager Robert Stansky.
"It's a combination of those things," one trader said.
IBM helped spark an uptick in the Dow, which climbed 37 to 6349, after falling back earlier.

Merrill's Mandresh raised his price target to $195 over the next 12 months, from a previous target of about $155. Mandresh cited his preliminary checks for the computer giant's fourth quarter outlook as helping in his latest assessment.

"IBM is a bellwether for the market which has been roaring along but just because it's trading at levels near before the '87 crash doesnt mean we're going into a tailspin anytime soon," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "Mandresh is considered to be Mr. IBM, so when he talks, investors listen."
John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst, also said he remains bullish on IBM.

"I'm very bullish on their outlook," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst, who has a price target of $155 to $160 for IBM in the next nine to 12 months. "Valuations between my number and his number (Mandresh's) are not unreasonable if the company continues to execute (on its strategic plans)."

Some analysts were a little cautious on IBM's surge, pointing out that the stock has climbed from about $90 in July to its current range of $143-$144. One market technician said, however, that the primary trend in IBM's stock remains up.
"I think the primary trend remains up," said Greg Nie, technical analyst at Everen Securities. "The stock is getting a little extended on a short-term basis."
Market technicians predict stock moves purely on the basis of charts and not based on company fundamentals.

According to Mandresh, IBM is on track for fourth quarter revenue growth of 10 percent to his estimate of $24 billion in revenues. "We are confident that if IBM achieves our 10 percent revenue growth forecast, gross margins can improve a point versus third quarter and thus come within a 1/2 point of last year's very strong 41.9 percent," he said.

Mandresh maintains his 1996 earnings estimate of $11.50 a share. He said IBM's U.S. business is doing well and on track for 10 percent revenue growth, he sees improvement in Europe (which has been in decline) and he is forecasting 2.5 percent growth in Europe. He also forecast 18 percent revenue growth in Asia Pacific and 11 percent growth in Latin America.

"From a product and revenue standpoint, the shining stars are services and PCs, with both areas likely to match Q3's spectacular growth of 25 percent," Mandresh said. He also said the company's high-end CMOS mainframes are sold out.
Therese Poletti 212/859-1728. Betty Wong also contributed.
